utterances.text: Well, sir, that's your opinion. Can you tell me -- well, the document speaks for itself. In terms of tab 13, this was an order signed -- purporting to be signed by Blaskic. You know, sir, don't you, that Colonel Blaskic at that time was in Kiseljak. He could not have signed an order in Vitez because he was in Kiseljak at the end of January 1993, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. But, Your Honours, it is really -- it was the chief of staff who signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did he do that with the agreement of Mr. Blaskic or Colonel Blaskic or do you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I am confident that he had to have. He could not have the authority of the commander for such orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry that he did not have?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, when you have this kind of order, the chief of staff could not but have the consent, the authority of the commander of the Operative Zone Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you'd agree then, sir, that in this particular instance, the fact that there -- someone like Colonel Blaskic, in this instance, was not physically present, doesn't mean that he or any other authority could not issue orders or authorisations by telephone or other communications; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: He could only give consent to carry out such and such order by telephone, that is, if the commander is absent, then the first man ranking below him had to do it because it had to get the green light if it was to be signed. And in this case, it is Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning for a moment to tab 15, my final question on these documents before moving forward. Sir, do you have any personal knowledge that Mr. Kordic did not, in fact, give Mr. Marin the agreement that he had asked for? Do you have any reason to tell us, on personal knowledge, that in fact, Colonel Kordic didn't do exactly as Slavko Marin asked him to do and indicate his agreement with this order?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marin, in this case, merely communicated with Colonel Blaskic, with the commander of the Operative Zone Central Bosnia. And basically, he did not -- he was not authorised to act by passing over orders except those which are enclosed. I don't think that he would be the head of the operations for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when were you first contacted by anyone working for the Defence of Mr. Kordic in connection with being a witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the communication -- the first communication with Dario Kordic's lawyer was in 1998; that is, we simply met. And a month and a half ago we were together in the area of Busovaca and talked about whether I would come to testify if such a need arose, and I gave my consent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between 1998 and approximately a month and a half ago, did you have any other contact with anyone on behalf of Mr. Kordic concerning his defence?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I do not recall such contact, and the first contact was in the case of Mr. Nobilo's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what steps did you take, if any, to prepare to testify today? Did you review any documents? Do you have a personal journal? Did you do anything to prepare yourself for coming to testify to this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I came here, that was the first time that I took the documents and papers to inspect them, to see them, and to gain additional knowledge to what I already was aware of. Before that, I did not have -- nor did I have any source which I could use to prepare myself, nor did I know the thesis about which the case could be conducted, at least not in great detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, touching briefly on paragraph 4 of your statement, you mention receiving training in Croatia for six months. Approximately when was that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the training -- I attended this commanding school, the officers' school, in 1996, between August 1996 until the end of July 1997. I went there from the post of the head of the chief of staff of the brigade and I went back to become the deputy commander of the 3rd Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on, I have a few minutes to touch on a few things before the end of the day. The flag-raising incident in February that you've been asked about, sir, in paragraph 34, you say you dimly recall this, and in paragraph 35, your testimony essentially is that you never heard information that Mr. Kordic had a role. Sir, I put it to you that you really have no knowledge, no personal information about this matter at all, do you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. During the briefing that we had in the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, that is, when I communicated with the chief of staff, I was told that during the night it had been taken off by the members of the security of Vitez with the approval of Colonel Blaskic. But I know that Mr. Kordic definitely had nothing to do with it, unless --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's not what you said in your statement. And before we get to that, you say you dimly recall, and then ultimately, in the latter part of paragraph 34, you say, "cannot remember anything clear." Now, did you write this? Is this your testimony? Was this your statement that you prepared or did somebody else put those words -- suggest those words to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm aware of what I said. I am aware, and I made my statement, that is, I prepared my statement with some support, that is, guidelines by the lawyers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What kind of guidelines did you receive from the lawyers about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I was shown a large part of documents to go through and the thesis which might be in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what thesis? Were you suggested -- were you given a thesis that your testimony should follow?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't really suggested to me. The theses were roughly outlined to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, such as? Sir, if I can put it -- let me rephrase my question. Was it put to you that you should come here and the thesis was to say whatever was necessary; to essentially say that Mr. Kordic had no role in these matters, that he had no military power, and that's basically what you should come here and say. Is that what was put to you in so many words?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was not put to me in those words. What I was told was that it would be necessary for me to come and testify, which I had already accepted a month and a half ago. And when I arrived here, I was given the thesis, such as January 1993, my CV, details from the date of my birth to my place of residence, education, military schools, duties, and that is how I wrote it all down; such as April 1993, convoys. Basically, that is it. Had to do with the general, but that was largely six, seven, or even eight years, and I used as many documents as were available to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's about time. It may be that there's a problem with -- not a problem but a difficulty arising from the translation. "Thesis" has a particular meaning in English but it sounds as though the witness is talking about subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I absolutely allow for that, Your Honour. I had a couple of follow-up questions. That's a distinct possibility. But we can finish on that topic in the morning, unless the Chamber wants to finish it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might clarify, Your Honour - sorry for jumping in - apparently the word in Croatian, according to my Croatian-speaking colleague here, is "theme" not "thesis."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that may explain it. Mr. Scott, how long do you think you will be tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. The witness was forecast with cross-examination being a full day and we've just started, so I think it will take the morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could have a look at it overnight with a view to restricting that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then we can -- there are some housekeeping matters we've got to deal with. There's outstanding the Kordic documents. Mr. Sayers, if you would get that into order for us tomorrow, please, we can look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And may I just say, Mr. President, just on a tangent, I apologise for zeal surpassing courtesy earlier today and I've communicated my apologies to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need for apologies. The next matter is there's a motion which we've received from the Prosecution about adjudicated facts. I don't know if the Defence have had it yet. No need for a written response; we can deal with it orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Might I suggest, Mr. President, if it's acceptable to the Trial Chamber, we could just deal with that in our final submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we need to go that far, but we'll talk about that tomorrow. I don't know if there are any other outstanding matters. We've got to rule on the two bundles of exhibits which we haven't ruled on, but we will do that during the remainder of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else outstanding. All I know is that in order for -- we want our documents that we serve on Wednesday to be as complete as they can be, and therefore, from an entirely selfish point of view, the sooner we can know about the documents, obviously, the better, because otherwise it's going to be very difficult to have those new documents integrated. But I understand entirely the pressure that's on the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mikulicic, you've got three witnesses, haven't you, as I recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, we have only two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two. When do you think they'll be here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think we can manage them throughout tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll see how we get on. If we can, so much the better. We'll adjourn now. Brigadier Grubesic, could you be back, please, at half past nine tomorrow morning to conclude your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
